title: Venus et Iuno. Venatio. Fama
titleEn: The Pact, the Hunt, the Cave and Rumour — Aeneid IV.105–205
part: The Pact, the Hunt, the Cave and Rumour (IV.105–205)
about: Venus sees through Juno's offer, but answers as if she believed it: who would refuse, if only Jupiter allowed one city for Tyrians and Trojans? Juno takes up the task. Tomorrow, when Aeneas and Dido ride out to hunt, she will send a black storm of rain and hail; the company will scatter, and the queen and the Trojan leader will find the same cave. There she will be present and make the marriage. Venus nods and smiles at the trick. At dawn the hunt gathers, the Carthaginian chiefs wait at the door, and Dido comes out in purple and gold; Aeneas joins her, as beautiful as Apollo when he leaves Lycia for Delos, and the young Ascanius rides ahead hoping for a boar. Then the storm breaks. The party runs for shelter, and Dido and Aeneas reach one cave, where Earth and Juno, goddess of marriage, give the signal, lightning flashes, and the nymphs cry out from the mountain top. Virgil calls that day the first cause of death and of evils. Dido no longer hides her love; she calls it marriage, and so veils her fault with a name. Rumour (Fama) now takes the stage: a monster, swift, many-eyed, fed on lies as much as truth, she flies by night and perches by day, and she carries the news to the African king Iarbas, a son of Jupiter Hammon and one of Dido's rejected suitors. He had built a hundred temples to his father. Maddened by the story, he stands before the altars and prays to Jupiter with raised palms; the prayer follows in the next part.

sentences.t:
Olli—sensit enim simulata mente locutam,
quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras—
sic contra est ingressa Venus:
sentences.l:
To her — for she sensed her to have spoken with a feigned mind,
to turn the kingdom of Italy aside to Libyan shores —
thus in reply Venus began:
sentences.i: To her — for she sensed that Juno spoke with feigned intent, to turn the kingdom of Italy aside to Libya's shores — Venus replied:
sentences.n: 'Olli' is an archaic form of 'illi', dative, 'to her' (Juno); the sentence is held in suspense by a parenthesis between dashes ('sensit enim… oras'). 'simulata mente' is an ablative of manner, 'with a feigned mind'; 'locutam' (sc. 'esse') is the perfect infinitive of the deponent 'loquor', agreeing with an understood 'illam'. 'quo… averteret' is a purpose clause introduced by 'quo' (= 'ut eo'), 'so as to turn away'. 'sic… est ingressa' means 'began (to speak) thus'. Venus knows what Juno is after, but plays along. This line begins one of Greenough's paragraphs.

sentences.t:
“Quis talia demens
abnuat, aut tecum malit contendere bello,
si modo, quod memoras, factum fortuna sequatur.
sentences.l:
“Who, being mad, would refuse such things,
or prefer to contend with you in war,
if only fortune would follow the deed you speak of?
sentences.i: “What madman would refuse such terms, or choose to fight against you, if only fortune follows what you promise?
sentences.n: 'demens' agrees with 'quis' ('who, being mad'); 'abnuat' and 'malit' are potential subjunctives (not 'who does' but 'who would'), a rhetorical question. 'malit' is the present subjunctive of 'malo', 'would prefer', with the infinitive 'contendere'. 'si modo… sequatur' is a proviso, 'if only', with the subjunctive. 'quod memoras' is the plan Juno has described; 'factum' is that plan as a done deed, which fortune must 'follow' (back it). The opening quotation mark is Greenough's.

sentences.t:
Sed fatis incerta feror, si Iuppiter unam
esse velit Tyriis urbem Troiaque profectis,
miscerive probet populos, aut foedera iungi.
sentences.l:
But I am borne uncertain by the fates, whether Jupiter
would wish one city to be for the Tyrians and those from Troy,
or approve the peoples to be mixed, or treaties to be joined.
sentences.i: But the fates leave me unsure whether Jupiter will wish the Tyrians and the men from Troy to have one city, or approve a mixing of the peoples, or the joining of treaties.
sentences.n: 'incerta feror' is 'I am carried uncertain', i.e. I do not know. 'si… velit… probet' is an indirect question, 'whether', with the subjunctive. 'unam esse urbem' is an accusative and infinitive after 'velit'; 'Tyriis Troiaque profectis' is a dative of possession ('to the Tyrians and to those who have set out from Troy'), where 'profectis' is a perfect participle and 'Troia' an ablative of separation. 'miscerive' is the passive infinitive 'misceri' with the enclitic '-ve', 'or'; 'misceri populos' and 'foedera iungi' are both passive infinitives dependent on 'probet', 'approve that the peoples be mixed, or that treaties be joined'. Venus's real fear is that Jupiter has promised Rome to Aeneas's descendants, so that a mixed city would overturn the promise.

sentences.t: Tu coniunx tibi fas animum temptare precando.”
sentences.l: You are his wife; it is right for you to try his mind by praying.”
sentences.i: You are his wife; it is lawful for you to sound his mind with prayer.”
sentences.n: The copula is omitted: 'Tu (es) coniunx; tibi (est) fas'. 'tibi' is a dative with 'fas', 'it is right for you'; 'animum temptare' is the infinitive that 'fas' governs, 'to sound out his mind'; 'precando' is an ablative of the gerund, 'by praying'. Venus reminds Juno that, as Jupiter's wife, it is for her to approach him. The closing quotation mark is Greenough's.

sentences.t: “Perge; sequar”.
sentences.l: “Go on; I shall follow”.
sentences.i: “Go on; I shall follow your lead”.
sentences.n: A tiny reply: 'perge' is the imperative (of 'pergo'), 'go on'; 'sequar' is the future of the deponent 'sequor'. Greenough puts the full stop outside the closing mark. The speaker is Venus.

sentences.t: Tum sic excepit regia Iuno:
sentences.l: Then thus took up the speech royal Juno:
sentences.i: Then royal Juno took up the speech:
sentences.n: 'excepit' is 'caught up', the verb used for taking over a conversation. 'regia Iuno' — she is queen of the gods. A speech introduced by 'sic' + colon is the regular opening; the speech runs to line 127.

sentences.t:
“Mecum erit iste labor: nunc qua ratione, quod instat
confieri possit, paucis, adverte, docebo.
sentences.l:
“With me will be that labour: now by what means what is pressing
can be brought about, in few words, attend, I shall teach.
sentences.i: “That task will be mine. By what means the matter now pressing can be done, I shall explain in a few words; give me your attention.
sentences.n: 'Mecum erit iste labor' is 'that labour will be with me', i.e. it is mine to do. 'qua ratione… possit' is an indirect question depending on 'docebo'; 'quod instat' is the subject of 'confieri', the passive infinitive of 'conficio', 'to be accomplished', which stands as the passive of 'conficere'. 'paucis' = 'paucis verbis' (ablative); 'adverte' = 'adverte animum', 'attend'. The speech is brisk and businesslike.

sentences.t:
Venatum Aeneas unaque miserrima Dido
in nemus ire parant, ubi primos crastinus ortus
extulerit Titan, radiisque retexerit orbem.
sentences.l:
To hunt Aeneas and together with him the most wretched Dido
are preparing to go into the wood, when tomorrow's Titan
has raised the first risings and has uncovered the world with rays.
sentences.i: Aeneas, and with him Dido, most wretched, are making ready to hunt in the wood, as soon as tomorrow's Titan has brought up the first sunrise and laid the world bare with his beams.
sentences.n: 'Venatum' is a supine in '-um', expressing purpose after a verb of motion ('ire'), 'to hunt'. 'Aeneas' is the subject of 'parant', plural with 'Dido' added after it. 'miserrima' is Juno's spiteful emphasis: 'most wretched' — Dido is already doomed. 'ubi… extulerit… retexerit' are future perfects, 'when… shall have raised… shall have uncovered'. 'Titan' is the Sun (Helios), a descendant of the Titans; 'ortus' is the plural, the first risings. 'radiis' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
His ego nigrantem commixta grandine nimbum,
dum trepidant alae, saltusque indagine cingunt,
desuper infundam, et tonitru caelum omne ciebo.
sentences.i: On them, while the riders hurry and the huntsmen ring the glades with a net, I shall pour a blackening cloud from above, thick with hail, and stir the whole sky with thunder.
sentences.n: 'His' is a dative, 'upon them'; 'nigrantem… nimbum' (a darkening cloud) is framed with 'commixta grandine' (ablative, 'mixed with hail'). 'dum trepidant' is 'dum' with the present indicative, 'while'. 'alae' are the wings of the hunting party, the riders; 'indagine' is the ring of nets used to enclose game; 'saltus' are wooded glades. 'infundam' and 'ciebo' are futures; 'tonitru' (thunder) is an ablative of means. 'ciebo' = 'I shall rouse'.

sentences.t: Diffugient comites et nocte tegentur opaca:
sentences.l: They will scatter, the companions, and by night will be covered, dark:
sentences.i: The company will scatter and be covered by dark night:
sentences.n: Future passive 'tegentur' follows the future 'diffugient'; 'nocte… opaca' is an ablative of means, 'darkness' (night in the middle of the day). The colon prepares the main point.

sentences.t:
speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem
devenient;
sentences.l:
Dido and the Trojan leader to the same cave
will come;
sentences.i: Dido and the Trojan chief will come to the same cave;
sentences.n: 'speluncam… eandem' is the accusative of the place to which, with no preposition, with 'devenient' (future of 'devenio'). 'dux' serves both subjects: 'Dido dux' and 'Troianus (dux)'. Line 165 repeats this line with one change: the verb is present, 'deveniunt' — the prophecy is fulfilled in the words that promised it.

sentences.t:
adero, et, tua si mihi certa voluntas,
[conubio iungam stabili propriamque dicabo,]
hic hymenaeus erit.”—Non adversata petenti
adnuit, atque dolis risit Cytherea repertis.
sentences.l:
I shall be there, and, if for me your will is sure,
[in a lasting marriage I shall join them and consecrate her as his own,]
this will be the wedding.”—Not having opposed her as she asked,
she assented, and Cytherea laughed at the wiles discovered.
sentences.i: I shall be there, and if your will holds firm for me, [I shall join them in lasting marriage and consecrate her as his own,] this shall be their wedding.” — Venus did not resist her entreaty; she nodded assent and laughed to see the wiles discovered.
sentences.n: 'adero' is the future of 'adsum', 'I shall be present'. 'tua si mihi certa voluntas' has 'est' omitted: 'if your will is firm to me'. Line 126 is printed in square brackets in Greenough, who marks it as spurious; we keep it, as the edition does. Without it, 'hic hymenaeus erit' follows directly on 'voluntas'. 'conubio stabili' is an ablative of means; 'propriam' is a predicate adjective, 'as his own'; 'dicabo' is 'I shall dedicate'. 'hymenaeus' is the wedding song, and so the wedding itself. The closing quotation mark is Greenough's. The dash separates the narrative from the speech. 'adversata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'adversor', 'having opposed', with the negative; 'petenti' is a dative of the present participle, 'to her asking' (Juno). 'adnuit' is 'nodded', i.e. agreed. 'Cytherea' is Venus, from the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have risen from the sea. 'dolis repertis' is an ablative absolute, 'the tricks having been found out': Venus sees that Juno is scheming, and smiles at it. A paragraph ends here.

sentences.t: Oceanum interea surgens Aurora reliquit.
sentences.l: Meanwhile rising Aurora left Ocean.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Dawn rose and left the Ocean behind.
sentences.n: 'Oceanum' is the river or sea that surrounds the earth in old geography, from which the sun and dawn come. 'surgens' is a present participle, 'as she rises'; Aurora is the goddess of dawn. This line begins a paragraph.

sentences.t: It portis iubare exorto delecta iuventus;
sentences.l: Through the gates, the light having risen, goes the chosen youth;
sentences.i: As the light rises, a chosen band of young men goes out through the gates;
sentences.n: 'It' is the present of 'eo', 'goes'; 'portis' is an ablative of the way out. 'iubare exorto' is an ablative absolute: 'iubar' is a beam of light, the sunrise. 'delecta iuventus' is a collective, 'picked young men', singular in form but plural in sense.

sentences.t:
retia rara, plagae, lato venabula ferro,
Massylique ruunt equites et odora canum vis.
sentences.l:
wide-meshed nets, snares, hunting spears with broad iron,
and the Massylian horsemen rush, and the keen-scented strength of hounds.
sentences.i: Wide-meshed nets, snares, broad-bladed hunting spears; the Massylian horsemen come at a run, and a keen-scented pack of hounds.
sentences.n: The first line is a list with no verb: 'retia rara' (the nets have wide meshes), 'plagae' (snares), 'venabula' (boar spears). 'ruunt' belongs to 'equites' and, loosely, to the rest. The Massyli are a Numidian people of North Africa, famed as horsemen. 'odora canum vis' is a periphrasis, 'the scenting strength of dogs' (singular 'vis' for the whole pack); 'canum' is the genitive plural of 'canis' (an '-um', not '-ium', ending).

sentences.t:
Reginam thalamo cunctantem ad limina primi
Poenorum exspectant, ostroque insignis et auro
stat sonipes, ac frena ferox spumantia mandit.
sentences.l:
The queen, lingering in her chamber, at the threshold the first
of the Phoenicians await, and, conspicuous with purple and gold,
stands her stamping horse, and fierce chews the foaming bit.
sentences.i: At the threshold the chiefs of Carthage wait for the queen, who lingers in her chamber; and her horse, bright in purple and gold, stands there and fiercely champs its foaming bit.
sentences.n: The word order frames the sentence around Dido: 'Reginam… cunctantem' (still lingering, delayed) is the object of 'exspectant', and 'primi Poenorum' is 'the first (chief) men of the Carthaginians'; 'Poenorum' is the genitive plural of 'Poeni', here the Carthaginians (Phoenician settlers). 'ostro… et auro' is an ablative of respect, 'conspicuous in purple and gold'. 'sonipes' ('noisy-footed') is a poetic noun for a horse. 'ferox' agrees with 'sonipes'; 'mandit' is 'chews'.

sentences.t:
Tandem progreditur, magna stipante caterva,
Sidoniam picto chlamydem circumdata limbo.
sentences.l:
At last she comes forth, a great crowd pressing round,
wrapped in a Sidonian cloak with an embroidered border.
sentences.i: At last she comes out, a great crowd pressing about her, wrapped in a Sidonian cloak with an embroidered border.
sentences.n: 'magna stipante caterva' is an ablative absolute, 'a great throng crowding around'. 'circumdata' is a perfect passive participle with a middle sense: 'having put around herself' — and the thing put on stays in the accusative, 'chlamydem' (a Greek retained accusative). 'Sidoniam' means Phoenician or Tyrian; Dido came from Tyre. 'picto limbo' is an ablative of quality, 'with an embroidered edge'.

sentences.t:
Cui pharetra ex auro, crines nodantur in aurum,
aurea purpuream subnectit fibula vestem.
sentences.l:
She has a quiver of gold, her hair is knotted into gold,
a golden brooch fastens her purple dress.
sentences.i: Her quiver is of gold, her hair is knotted up in gold, a golden clasp pins her purple dress.
sentences.n: 'Cui pharetra ex auro' is a dative of possession with 'est' omitted: 'to her (is) a quiver of gold'; 'cui' is a connecting relative, 'she has'. 'nodantur in aurum' is passive, 'are knotted into gold'. The word 'gold' returns three times (auro, aurum, aurea), set against 'purpuream'. 'subnectit' is 'fastens below' (the brooch pins the dress at the shoulder).

sentences.t:
Nec non et Phrygii comites et laetus Iulus
incedunt.
sentences.l:
Nor less do the Phrygian companions and glad Iulus
walk on.
sentences.i: The Trojan companions and glad Iulus advance too.
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' is a strong linking phrase, 'and also'. 'Phrygii' means Trojan, Phrygia being the region of Troy in a loose sense. 'Iulus' is Ascanius, Aeneas's son. The verb 'incedunt' is plural, agreeing with both 'comites' and 'Iulus'; it describes a stately walking, 'march in procession'.

sentences.t:
Ipse ante alios pulcherrimus omnis
infert se socium Aeneas atque agmina iungit.
sentences.l:
He himself, most beautiful before all the others,
brings himself as a companion, Aeneas, and joins the columns.
sentences.i: Aeneas himself, fairest of them all, brings himself to her side and joins the columns together.
sentences.n: 'omnis' is the accusative plural in '-is' (for 'omnes') and agrees with 'alios': 'ante alios… omnis' is 'before all the others'; 'pulcherrimus' agrees with 'Aeneas', held to the end of the next line. 'infert se' is the idiom 'brings himself in', to enter, here as Dido's partner ('socium'). 'agmina iungit' is 'joins the lines together', Trojan and Tyrian.

sentences.t:
Qualis ubi hibernam Lyciam Xanthique fluenta
deserit ac Delum maternam invisit Apollo,
instauratque choros, mixtique altaria circum
Cretesque Dryopesque fremunt pictique Agathyrsi;
sentences.l:
Such as when Apollo leaves wintry Lycia and the streams of Xanthus
and visits his mother's Delos,
and renews the dances, and around the altars mingled
Cretans and Dryopes shout, and the painted Agathyrsi;
sentences.i: As Apollo is when he forsakes Lycia, his winter home, and the flowing waters of the Xanthus, and goes to Delos, his mother's isle, and sets the dances going again, while Cretans, Dryopes and painted Agathyrsians, thronging round, cry out about the altars;
sentences.n: The long simile begins with 'Qualis ubi… Apollo', 'just as when Apollo…', and is completed in 149–150 ('haud illo segnior ibat Aeneas'). Apollo was said to spend the winter in Lycia (Asia Minor, by the river Xanthus) and to return each spring to his birthplace Delos, 'maternam' because his mother Latona bore him there. 'instaurat choros' is 'renews the choral dances'. 'Cretes', 'Dryopes' and 'Agathyrsi' are peoples who share the island's festival; the Agathyrsi (a Scythian people) were said to paint their bodies. 'altaria circum' has the preposition after its noun (anastrophe). 'fremunt' is 'roar, shout'.

sentences.t:
ipse iugis Cynthi graditur, mollique fluentem
fronde premit crinem fingens atque implicat auro;
sentences.l:
He himself walks on the ridges of Cynthus, and the flowing
hair presses with soft leaves, shaping it, and entwines it with gold;
sentences.i: He himself walks the ridges of Cynthus, and, shaping his flowing hair, presses it down under soft foliage and twines it with gold;
sentences.n: 'Cynthi' belongs to Mount Cynthus on Delos, from which Apollo is 'Cynthius'. 'ipse' resumes the subject, Apollo, with a fresh main verb, 'graditur'. 'mollique fronde… crinem' interlock: 'premit' is 'presses down', 'fingens' (participle) is 'shaping, dressing', and 'implicat' is 'entwines'. 'fronde' and 'auro' are ablatives of means: a wreath of leaves with gold.

sentences.t: tela sonant umeris:
sentences.l: the arrows ring on his shoulders:
sentences.i: the arrows ring on his shoulders:
sentences.n: 'tela sonant umeris': 'umeris' is an ablative of place, 'on his shoulders'; the arrows rattle in the quiver as he walks. The colon leads to the comparison with Aeneas.

sentences.t:
haud illo segnior ibat
Aeneas;
sentences.l:
not slower than he went
Aeneas;
sentences.i: Aeneas went with no less spring in his step;
sentences.n: 'haud illo segnior' is 'not more sluggish than he', an ablative of comparison ('illo'). The simile is closed: Aeneas as the god. 'ibat' is the imperfect of 'eo'. The name 'Aeneas' is held back to the end of the sentence for emphasis.

sentences.t: tantum egregio decus enitet ore.
sentences.l: so great a glory shines out from his noble face.
sentences.i: such beauty shines out from his noble face.
sentences.n: 'tantum' is neuter singular and agrees with 'decus', 'so great'; 'enitet' is 'shines out' (from 'eniteo'). 'egregio ore' is an ablative of source, 'from his noble face'; 'decus' is 'glory, grace'.

sentences.i: When they came to the high mountains and pathless lairs, see, wild goats, shaken loose from the crag's peak, ran down the ridges;
sentences.n: 'Postquam altos ventum in montis' is an impersonal passive: 'it was come to the high mountains' (we would say 'they came'); 'montis' is accusative plural in '-is'. 'invia lustra' are the pathless lairs of wild beasts. 'ecce' calls attention. 'saxi vertice' is an ablative of separation, 'from the top of a rock'. 'decurrere' = 'decurrerunt' (the '-ere' for '-erunt', as flagged earlier). 'iugis' is an ablative of the way, 'along the ridges'.

sentences.t:
alia de parte patentis
transmittunt cursu campos atque agmina cervi
pulverulenta fuga glomerant montisque relinquunt.
sentences.l:
on another side the stags across the open plains
cross at a run, and bunch their dusty columns in flight,
and leave the mountains.
sentences.i: On another side the stags run across the open plains, and in their flight gather into dusty herds, and leave the mountains behind.
sentences.n: 'patentis' is an accusative plural for 'patentes' (open). 'transmittunt cursu' is 'send across by running', i.e. cross. 'pulverulenta' (dusty) agrees with 'agmina', and 'fuga' is an ablative, 'in flight'; 'glomerant' is 'gather into clusters'. 'cervi' is the subject of all three verbs, delayed to the end of its clause. 'montis' is again an accusative plural.

sentences.t:
At puer Ascanius mediis in vallibus acri
gaudet equo, iamque hos cursu, iam praeterit illos,
spumantemque dari pecora inter inertia votis
optat aprum, aut fulvum descendere monte leonem.
sentences.l:
But the boy Ascanius in the middle of the valleys with his eager
horse rejoices, and now these at a run, now those he rides past,
and among the sluggish cattle, a foaming boar to be given
he prays for in his vows, or a tawny lion to come down from the mountain.
sentences.i: But the boy Ascanius, down in the valleys, revels in his spirited horse, and now overtakes some at a gallop, now others, and wishes that, among the idle herds, a foaming boar would be given to his prayers, or a tawny lion come down from the hills.
sentences.n: 'acri equo' is an ablative with 'gaudet', 'rejoices in'. 'hos… illos' is 'some… others', the object of 'praeterit', 'passes, outstrips'. 'optat' takes two accusative and infinitive phrases: 'spumantem aprum dari' ('a boar to be given') and 'fulvum leonem descendere' ('a lion to come down'). 'pecora inter inertia' is anastrophe (preposition after its noun): 'among the sluggish cattle', the unwarlike herds. 'votis' goes with 'dari', 'to be given to his vows' (in answer to them); it may be read as dative or ablative, with little change of sense.

sentences.t:
Interea magno misceri murmure caelum
incipit;
sentences.l:
Meanwhile with a great rumbling to be mingled the sky
begins;
sentences.i: Meanwhile the sky begins to churn with a great rumbling;
sentences.n: 'misceri' is the passive infinitive after 'incipit', 'begins to be mixed (confused)'. 'magno murmure' is an ablative of manner. This line begins a paragraph: the storm Juno promised.

sentences.t: insequitur commixta grandine nimbus;
sentences.l: there follows a cloud mixed with hail;
sentences.i: a cloud follows, charged with hail;
sentences.n: 'commixta grandine' echoes line 120 ('commixta grandine nimbum') exactly: what Juno said she would do, she does. Virgil repeats her words in the action, as he does with line 124 at line 165.

sentences.i: and the Tyrian company, the young Trojans and Venus's Dardan grandson sought shelter in terror, each a different way, across the fields;
sentences.n: 'passim' is 'on every side'. 'Dardanius nepos Veneris' is Ascanius ('Dardanius' = Trojan, 'nepos' = grandson). 'diversa' agrees with 'tecta': shelters in different directions; 'tecta' are roofs, shelters. 'metu' is an ablative of cause. 'petiere' = 'petiverunt'. 'per agros' = 'over the fields'. The long subject is held in suspense until the verb.

sentences.t: ruunt de montibus amnes.
sentences.l: torrents rush down from the mountains.
sentences.i: streams come rushing down the mountains.
sentences.n: 'ruunt' again, as in 132: 'rush'. 'amnes' is the subject, 'rivers' (here flash floods). 'de montibus' is 'down from the mountains'. This short unit closes the sentence begun at 162, whose verb 'petiere' stands in the line before.

sentences.t:
Speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem
deveniunt:
sentences.l:
To the same cave Dido and the Trojan leader
come:
sentences.i: Dido and the Trojan chief come to the same cave:
sentences.n: A word-for-word return of line 124, with 'deveniunt' (present) for 'devenient' (future). Juno said it would happen, and now it does.

sentences.t:
prima et Tellus et pronuba Iuno
dant signum;
sentences.l:
first both Earth and the bridal Juno
give the sign;
sentences.i: Earth first, and Juno, goddess of marriage, give the sign;
sentences.n: 'prima' is nominative feminine, agreeing with 'Tellus', the nearer subject, but English takes it as an adverb: 'first'. 'Tellus' is Earth, mother of all. 'pronuba Iuno' — 'pronuba' is the matron who attends the bride; Juno is the goddess of marriage (Iuno Pronuba). 'dant signum' is the sign for the ceremony to begin.

sentences.t:
fulsere ignes et conscius aether
conubiis, summoque ulularunt vertice nymphae.
sentences.l:
the fires flashed and the sky, a witness
to the marriage, and on the highest peak the nymphs wailed.
sentences.i: lightnings flashed, and the sky, a witness to the marriage, and the nymphs cried out from the mountain's crest.
sentences.n: 'fulsere' = 'fulserunt'. 'ignes' are lightning flashes (and the wedding torches in a metaphorical sense). 'conscius aether' — the upper air as a witness; 'conubiis' is a dative with 'conscius', 'aware of the marriage'. 'ulularunt' = 'ululaverunt', the ritual wail of women, here the nymphs of the hills taking the part of the bridal cry. The only witnesses at this wedding are powers of nature.

sentences.t:
Ille dies primus leti primusque malorum
causa fuit;
sentences.l:
That day, first of death and first of evils,
the cause was;
sentences.i: That day was the first cause of death, and the first cause of evils;
sentences.n: 'Ille dies primus leti primusque malorum causa fuit': 'primus' is masculine, agreeing with 'dies' ('that day… first'), and 'causa' is the predicate noun, understood again with 'malorum'; 'leti' and 'malorum' are genitives dependent on 'causa'. The poet speaks outright, in his own voice: Dido's suicide and the long enmity of Carthage and Rome are the 'evils'.

sentences.t:
neque enim specie famave movetur,
nec iam furtivum Dido meditatur amorem:
sentences.l:
for neither by appearance nor by repute is she moved,
nor now does Dido plan a secret love:
sentences.i: for she is no longer troubled by appearance or by what is said of her, nor does Dido now plan a stealthy love:
sentences.n: 'specie famave' is an ablative of cause, 'by appearance or reputation' — she is no longer concerned for her good name. 'fama' is introduced here as a human quantity; in a few lines it becomes a goddess-monster. 'iam' with the negative is 'no longer'. 'furtivum amorem' is 'stolen love', affair in secret.

sentences.t: coniugium vocat;
sentences.l: she calls it marriage;
sentences.i: she calls it marriage;
sentences.n: 'coniugium' is the predicate accusative after 'vocat', with 'amorem' understood as its object: 'she calls it marriage'. The colon after 'amorem' in the previous line leads into it.

sentences.t: hoc praetexit nomine culpam.
sentences.l: with this name she veils her fault.
sentences.i: with this name she cloaks her fault.
sentences.n: 'praetexit' is 'weaves in front, covers' (cf. 'toga praetexta', the bordered toga); 'hoc nomine' is an ablative of means, 'with this name'; 'culpam' is her 'fault', in Virgil's own word.

sentences.t: Extemplo Libyae magnas it Fama per urbes—
sentences.l: At once through the great cities of Libya goes Rumour —
sentences.i: At once Rumour goes through the great cities of Libya —
sentences.n: 'Extemplo' is 'immediately'. 'Fama' is both 'report, rumour' and 'reputation, fame'; here it becomes a personification, introduced with a dash. This line begins a paragraph, and the famous passage on Fama.

sentences.t: Fama, malum qua non aliud velocius ullum;
sentences.l: Rumour, than which no other evil is any faster;
sentences.i: Rumour, an evil swifter than any other;
sentences.n: 'malum' is in apposition to 'Fama' ('an evil'); 'qua' is an ablative of comparison with 'velocius', 'than which'. 'non aliud… ullum' is a pleonastic negative for emphasis: 'no other evil… any quicker'.

sentences.t:
mobilitate viget, viresque adquirit eundo,
parva metu primo, mox sese attollit in auras,
ingrediturque solo, et caput inter nubila condit.
sentences.l:
by mobility she thrives, and gains strength by going,
small at first through fear, soon lifts herself into the air
and walks upon the ground, and her head among the clouds hides.
sentences.i: She flourishes on movement and wins strength from her going: small at first, from fear, she soon lifts herself into the air, treads the ground, and hides her head among the clouds.
sentences.n: 'mobilitate' is an ablative of cause or means, 'by (her) swiftness'; 'eundo' is the gerund in the ablative, 'by going'. Greenough reads 'viresque' where the Latin Library prints 'virisque'. 'parva metu primo' — 'parva' is nominative feminine and 'metu' an ablative of cause, 'small at first through fear' (whether her own fear or the fear she will cause is debated). 'ingreditur solo' is 'walks on the ground', with an ablative of place. 'caput inter nubila condit' has anastrophe.

sentences.t:
Illam Terra parens, ira inritata deorum,
extremam (ut perhibent) Coeo Enceladoque sororem
progenuit, pedibus celerem et pernicibus alis,
sentences.l:
Her Earth the parent, provoked by anger at the gods,
last sister (as they say) of Coeus and Enceladus
bore, swift in feet and in quick wings,
sentences.i: Earth, her mother, roused by resentment against the gods, bore her (so the tale goes) as a last sister to Coeus and Enceladus, swift of foot and of quick wing,
sentences.n: 'Illam' (object) is held in front, then comes the subject 'Terra parens', and the verb 'progenuit' only in 180. 'ira inritata deorum' — 'deorum' is an objective genitive, 'anger against the gods'; Earth bore the Titans and Giants (Coeus was a Titan, Enceladus a Giant) who rebelled against the Olympians and lost. Fama is their last sister: 'extremam'. 'ut perhibent' is 'as they say', a hedge on a story that is hard to believe. 'pedibus celerem et pernicibus alis' is an ablative of respect.

sentences.t:
monstrum horrendum, ingens, cui, quot sunt corpore plumae
tot vigiles oculi subter, mirabile dictu,
tot linguae, totidem ora sonant, tot subrigit aures.
sentences.l:
a monster dreadful, huge, to whom, as many as are the feathers on her body,
so many watchful eyes beneath, wonderful to tell,
so many tongues, as many mouths sound, so many ears she pricks up.
sentences.i: a monster, dreadful and huge, who has as many wakeful eyes beneath as she has feathers on her body — a marvel to relate — as many tongues, as many sounding mouths, as many ears she pricks up.
sentences.n: 'quot… tot' and 'tot… totidem… tot' is a correlative set: 'as many… so many'. 'cui' is a dative of possession; 'sunt' belongs to the 'quot' clause, and 'subter' means 'beneath' (the eyes are under the feathers). 'mirabile dictu' uses the supine in '-u', 'wonderful to tell'. 'sonant' is used of the mouths, 'make sound'; 'subrigit' is 'pricks up'. A creature of eyes, tongues and ears is the picture of gossip.

sentences.t:
Nocte volat caeli medio terraeque per umbram,
stridens, nec dulci declinat lumina somno;
sentences.l:
By night she flies in the middle of heaven and earth through the shadow,
screeching, nor does she lower her eyes in sweet sleep;
sentences.i: By night she flies between heaven and earth through the darkness, shrieking, and never lets her eyes sink in sweet sleep;
sentences.n: 'caeli medio terraeque' is 'in the middle (space) of sky and earth', with 'medio' as a noun and two genitives; 'per umbram' is 'through the darkness'. 'stridens' is the present participle, 'shrieking'. 'declinat lumina somno' is 'she lowers her eyes in sleep', with 'somno' an ablative of means (some read a dative, 'to sleep'); 'dulci' is the conventional epithet.

sentences.t:
luce sedet custos aut summi culmine tecti,
turribus aut altis, et magnas territat urbes;
sentences.l:
by day she sits as a watcher on a roof's summit
or on high towers, and terrifies the great cities;
sentences.i: By day she sits on guard at the peak of a roof or on lofty towers, and frightens great cities;
sentences.n: 'luce' is an ablative of time, 'by daylight' (as 'nocte' in 184). 'summi culmine tecti' is 'on the peak of the highest roof': 'summi' agrees with 'tecti', the roof being the highest part. 'turribus altis' is another ablative of place, 'aut' links the two. 'custos' is a predicative noun, 'as a guard'.

sentences.t: tam ficti pravique tenax, quam nuntia veri.
sentences.l: as tenacious of the false and the perverse as messenger of the true.
sentences.i: She clings to what is false and twisted as firmly as she carries word of what is true.
sentences.n: 'tenax' takes the genitive ('ficti pravique'), 'tenacious of, clinging to'. 'tam… quam' is 'as much… as'. 'nuntia' is the feminine noun 'messenger', in apposition to 'Fama' and predicative; 'veri' is its genitive. The paragraph, and the description, end.

sentences.t:
Haec tum multiplici populos sermone replebat
gaudens, et pariter facta atque infecta canebat:
sentences.l:
This, then, with manifold talk the peoples she was filling,
rejoicing, and alike things done and things not done she told:
sentences.i: Then she filled the peoples with her many-voiced talk, delighted, and told alike of deeds done and deeds undone:
sentences.n: 'Haec' is the subject (Fama); 'tum' is 'at that time'. 'multiplici sermone' is an ablative of means, 'with her many-fold talk'. 'replebat' and 'canebat' are imperfects of repeated action. 'facta atque infecta' — 'done and undone', what happened and what did not. 'canebat' is the verb of the poet's own song (line 1, 'cano'). This line begins a paragraph. The colon introduces her message in indirect speech.

sentences.t:
venisse Aenean, Troiano sanguine cretum,
cui se pulchra viro dignetur iungere Dido;
sentences.l:
that Aeneas had come, born of Trojan blood,
to whom, as husband, the fair Dido deigns to join herself;
sentences.i: that Aeneas had come, sprung from Trojan blood, and that fair Dido deigns to take him as her husband;
sentences.n: The report is in indirect speech: the accusative and infinitive 'venisse Aenean' ('Aenean' is the Greek accusative), then a relative clause with the subjunctive 'dignetur' (a subordinate verb in indirect speech). 'cretum' is the participle of 'cresco', 'sprung from'. 'cui' is a dative with 'iungere', 'to join herself to whom', and 'viro' is in apposition, 'as husband'; 'pulchra' is said of Dido.

sentences.t:
nunc hiemem inter se luxu, quam longa, fovere
regnorum immemores turpique cupidine captos.
sentences.l:
that now the winter between themselves, however long it is, they cherish in luxury,
forgetful of their kingdoms, and caught in shameful desire.
sentences.i: that now they pass the whole of the winter together in luxury, however long it is, forgetting their kingdoms, held captive by a base desire.
sentences.n: The indirect speech continues with infinitives: 'fovere' (here 'they cherish, spend warmly') takes 'hiemem' as its object. 'inter se' is 'with each other'. 'quam longa (sit)' is 'however long', a parenthetical clause with the verb omitted. 'regnorum immemores' takes the genitive; 'immemores' and 'captos' (accusative plural) agree with the unnamed pair, the subject accusative of 'fovere'. 'turpi cupidine' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t: Haec passim dea foeda virum diffundit in ora.
sentences.l: This, everywhere, the foul goddess spreads into the mouths of men.
sentences.i: These things the foul goddess spreads everywhere upon the lips of men.
sentences.n: 'dea foeda' — Virgil calls her a goddess; 'foeda' (foul) is a word of moral disgust. 'virum' is the old genitive plural for 'virorum'.

sentences.t:
Protinus ad regem cursus detorquet Iarban,
incenditque animum dictis atque aggerat iras.
sentences.l:
At once to King Iarbas she turns her course,
and inflames his mind with words and heaps up his rage.
sentences.i: At once she bends her course toward King Iarbas, kindles his heart with her words and piles up his anger.
sentences.n: 'Protinus' is 'straight on, at once'. 'cursus detorquet' is 'twists her course'. Iarbas is a Libyan king and one of the suitors Dido refused. 'dictis' is an ablative of means; 'aggerat' is 'heaps up' (from 'agger', a mound). Rumour thus carries the story out of the cave and into the world.

sentences.t:
Hic Hammone satus, rapta Garamantide Nympha,
templa Iovi centum latis immania regnis,
centum aras posuit, vigilemque sacraverat ignem,
excubias divom aeternas, pecudumque cruore
pingue solum et variis florentia limina sertis.
sentences.l:
He, sprung from Hammon, a Garamantian nymph having been carried off,
had set up to Jupiter a hundred temples huge in broad realms,
a hundred altars, and had consecrated a watching fire,
the eternal watches of the gods, and with the blood of animals
the soil fat, and the thresholds flowering with various garlands.
sentences.i: He, son of Hammon by a Garamantian nymph he had carried off, had set up to Jupiter a hundred vast temples in his broad realms, a hundred altars, and had hallowed a sleepless fire, the gods' everlasting vigil, the soil rich with the blood of beasts, and the doorways in bloom with garlands of every kind.
sentences.n: 'Hic' is Iarbas. 'Hammone satus' — 'satus' is 'sprung from' with the ablative of origin; Hammon is the Libyan god identified with Jupiter. 'rapta Garamantide Nympha' is an ablative absolute, 'a Garamantian nymph (having been) carried off': the Garamantes are a people of the Libyan desert. 'templa Iovi' — 'Iovi' is a dative of the recipient; 'centum… immania' is 'a hundred huge'; 'latis regnis' is an ablative of place. 'sacraverat' is the pluperfect, 'had consecrated'. 'vigilem ignem' is a never-extinguished fire; 'excubias' (nightly watches) is in apposition. 'divom' is Greenough's spelling of 'divum', the old genitive plural. 'pingue' and 'florentia' agree with 'solum' and 'limina', which are further accusative objects of 'sacraverat'; 'cruore' and 'sertis' are ablatives of means. This line begins a paragraph.

sentences.t:
Isque amens animi et rumore accensus amaro
dicitur ante aras media inter numina divom
multa Iovem manibus supplex orasse supinis:
sentences.l:
And he, out of his mind, and fired by bitter rumour,
is said before the altars, in the midst of the divinities of the gods,
to have prayed much to Jupiter, a suppliant, with his hands turned up:
sentences.i: Frantic, and fired by that bitter rumour, he is said to have prayed long to Jupiter, a suppliant before the altars, amid the powers of the gods, with upturned palms:
sentences.n: 'Isque' is 'and he', a connecting 'is'. 'amens animi' is 'out of his mind', with the genitive of respect ('animi'). 'rumore accensus amaro' is an ablative of means, 'inflamed by bitter rumour'. 'dicitur… orasse' is the personal use of 'dicitur' with the perfect infinitive 'orasse' = 'oravisse', 'is said to have prayed'. 'media inter numina divom' has anastrophe: 'amid the powers of the gods', with 'divom' for 'divum'. 'supinis manibus' means 'with hands turned palm up', the usual Roman gesture of prayer. 'multa' is a neuter plural used adverbially, 'at length'. The colon leads into his prayer in the next part.
